Appendix D Analysis of the Practical Gradient Estimator from Algorithm 1

In this section, we will analyse the practical gradient estimator from Algorithm 1, which includes both an unconditional average score baseline to reduce variance, and sets the gradient to be 0 in the case of all negative rollouts (no baseline is used). We show that this changes the objective for which the gradient is unbiased for: while the gradient from Eq. 9 is unbiased for the MaxRL gradient of order T=NT=N (Theorem 2), the practical gradient estimator is instead unbiased for the MaxRL gradient of order T=N−1T=N-1. We formally prove this result below.

Theorem 5 (Effective truncation of the dropped-baseline estimator).

Fix an input xx and let z1,…,zN∼mθ(⋅∣x)z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) be NN i.i.d. rollouts from the latent policy. Define

ri=𝕀{f(zi)=y∗(x)},K=∑i=1Nri,Si=∇θlogmθ(zi∣x).r_{i}=\mathbb{I}\{f(z_{i})=y^{\ast}(x)\},\qquad K=\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{i},\qquad S_{i}=\nabla_{\theta}\log m_{\theta}(z_{i}\mid x).

Let

pθpass(x)=ℙz∼mθ(⋅∣x)(f(z)=y∗(x)),p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)=\mathbb{P}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}(f(z)=y^{\ast}(x)),

and assume the standard score-function identities

𝔼⁡[Si]=0,𝔼⁡[ri​Si]=∇θpθpass​(x).\mathbb{E}[S_{i}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[r_{i}S_{i}]=\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x).

Consider the practical gradient estimator from Algorithm 1

g~N(x)=𝕀{K>0}(1K∑i=1NriSi−1N∑i=1NSi).\widetilde{g}_{N}(x)=\mathbb{I}\{K>0\}\left(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{i}S_{i}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}\right).

Then

𝔼⁡[g~N​(x)]=∑t=1N−1(1−pθpass​(x))t−1​∇θpθpass​(x).\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{g}_{N}(x)]=\sum_{t=1}^{N-1}(1-p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x))^{t-1}\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x).

Equivalently, the practical dropped-baseline estimator is unbiased for the (N−1)(N-1)-truncated MaxRL gradient.

Proof. For readability, write p=pθpass​(x)p=p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x) and ∇p=∇θpθpass​(x)\nabla p=\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x). Decompose the estimator as

g~N​(x)=𝕀{K>0}1K∑i=1NriSi⏟g~Nsucc​(x)−𝕀{K>0}1N∑i=1NSi⏟g~Nbase​(x).\widetilde{g}_{N}(x)=\underbrace{\mathbb{I}\{K>0\}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{i}S_{i}}_{\widetilde{g}_{N}^{\mathrm{succ}}(x)}-\underbrace{\mathbb{I}\{K>0\}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}}_{\widetilde{g}_{N}^{\mathrm{base}}(x)}.

By the standard MaxRL estimator identity from Theorem 2, the successful-rollout term satisfies

𝔼[g~Nsucc(x)]=∑t=1N(1−p)t−1∇p.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widetilde{g}_{N}^{\mathrm{succ}}(x)\right]=\sum_{t=1}^{N}(1-p)^{t-1}\nabla p.

It remains to compute the expectation of the dropped baseline term. Since

𝔼⁡[1N​∑i=1NSi]=0,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}\right]=0,

we have

𝔼[𝕀{K>0}1N∑i=1NSi]=−𝔼[𝕀{K=0}1N∑i=1NSi].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{I}\{K>0\}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}\right]=-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{I}\{K=0\}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}\right].

Now observe that

𝕀{K=0}=∏ℓ=1N(1−rℓ).\mathbb{I}\{K=0\}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{N}(1-r_{\ell}).

Using independence of the samples,

𝔼[𝕀{K=0}1N∑i=1NSi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{I}\{K=0\}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}\right] =1N​∑i=1N𝔼⁡[(1−ri)​Si]​∏ℓ≠i𝔼⁡[1−rℓ]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(1-r_{i})S_{i}\right]\prod_{\ell\neq i}\mathbb{E}[1-r_{\ell}]
=1N​∑i=1N(𝔼⁡[Si]−𝔼⁡[ri​Si])​(1−p)N−1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\mathbb{E}[S_{i}]-\mathbb{E}[r_{i}S_{i}]\right)(1-p)^{N-1}
=−(1−p)N−1∇p.\displaystyle=-(1-p)^{N-1}\nabla p.

Therefore,

𝔼[g~Nbase(x)]=(1−p)N−1∇p.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widetilde{g}_{N}^{\mathrm{base}}(x)\right]=(1-p)^{N-1}\nabla p.

Combining the two terms gives

𝔼​[g~N​(x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{g}_{N}(x)] =[∑t=1N(1−p)t−1∇p]−(1−p)N−1∇p\displaystyle=\left[\sum_{t=1}^{N}(1-p)^{t-1}\nabla p\right]-(1-p)^{N-1}\nabla p
=∑t=1N−1(1−p)t−1∇p.\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{N-1}(1-p)^{t-1}\nabla p.

Substituting back p=pθpass​(x)p=p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x) yields

𝔼⁡[g~N​(x)]=∑t=1N−1(1−pθpass​(x))t−1​∇θpθpass​(x),\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{g}_{N}(x)]=\sum_{t=1}^{N-1}(1-p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x))^{t-1}\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x),

which is exactly the (N−1)(N-1)-truncated MaxRL gradient, concluding our proof. ∎

Appendix E More on Unifying Weight-Function View on RL Objectives

Here we provide full derivations following Section 5. Recall that we want to express population-level gradients of different objectives in the following form:

∇θJ=𝔼x∼ρ​[w⁡(pθ​(x))​∇θpθ​(x)]\nabla_{\theta}J=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[w(p_{\theta}(x))\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(x)\right]

where pθ​(x)=pθpass​(x)p_{\theta}(x)=p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x) and w​(pθ​(x))w(p_{\theta}(x)) is the weighting function. In this section, we show that all objectives of our consideration can be written in this form. Furthermore, we will derive the weighting function w​(pθ​(x))w(p_{\theta}(x)) for each of them.

Classical RL (REINFORCE)

For classical reinforcement learning, i.e., the REINFORCE objective, we have:

JRL=\displaystyle J_{\mathrm{RL}}={} 𝔼x∼ρ[𝔼z∼mθ(⋅|x)[r(x,z)]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}[\mathbb{E}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,z)]]
=\displaystyle={} 𝔼x∼ρ[𝔼z∼mθ(⋅|x)[𝕀{f(z)=y∗(x)}]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}[\mathbb{E}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[\mathbb{I}\left\{f(z)=y^{\ast}(x)\right\}]]
=\displaystyle={} 𝔼x∼ρ​[pθpass​(x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}[p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)]

Therefore, its gradient is:

∇θJRL=𝔼x∼ρ​[∇θpθpass​(x)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{RL}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}[\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)]

giving the corresponding wRLw_{\mathrm{RL}} to be 11.

GRPO

Our analysis is similar to that of Davis and Recht (2025). The gradient of the population level GRPO objective gradient can be written as:

∇θJGRPO=\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{GRPO}}={} 𝔼x∼ρ[𝔼z∼mθ(⋅|x)[(r(x,z)−𝔼z∼mθ(⋅|x)[r(x,z)]Varz∼mθ(⋅|x)[r(x,z)])∇θlogmθ(z|x)]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[\mathbb{E}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[\left(\frac{r(x,z)-\mathbb{E}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,z)]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,z)]}}\right)\nabla_{\theta}\log m_{\theta}(z|x)\right]\right]

Since we consider a binary reward setting, we have 𝔼z∼mθ(⋅|x)[r(x,z)]=pθpass(x)\mathbb{E}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,z)]=p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x). Similarly, considering the variance of a Bernoulli random variable, we get:

Varz∼mθ(⋅|x)[r(x,z)]=pθpass(x)(1−pθpass(x))\mathrm{Var}_{z\sim m_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,z)]=p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)\left(1-p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)\right)

Therefore, the objective becomes:

∇θJGRPO=𝔼x∼ρ​[1pθpass​(x)​(1−pθpass​(x))​∇θpθpass​(x)]\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)\left(1-p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)\right)}}\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)\right]

which thereby gives us the weighting function to be 1/pθ​(x)​(1−pθ​(x))1/\sqrt{p_{\theta}(x)(1-p_{\theta}(x))}, as desired.

Maximum Likelihood (ML)

The maximum likelihood objective is given by

JML=𝔼x∼ρ​[log⁡pθpass​(x)].J_{\mathrm{ML}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}[\log p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)].

Taking its gradient with respect to θ\theta and applying the chain rule, we obtain

∇θJML=\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{ML}}={} 𝔼x∼ρ​[∇θ​log​pθpass​(x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)\right]
=\displaystyle={} 𝔼x∼ρ​[1pθpass​(x)​∇θpθpass​(x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[\frac{1}{p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)}\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x)\right]

This shows that the weighting function for the maximum likelihood objective is 1/pθpass​(x)1/p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x), as we claimed in Fig. 1.

MaxRL

Finally, we consider the objective JMaxRL(T)J_{\mathrm{\textsc{MaxRL}}}^{(T)}.

Proposition 6.

For MaxRL with order TT, we can rewrite it as

∇θJMaxRL(T)=𝔼x∼ρ​[w⁡(pθ​(x))​∇θpθ​(x)],\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J^{(T)}_{\textsc{MaxRL}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\!\left[w\!\left(p_{\theta}(x)\right)\,\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(x)\right],

where

wT​(p)=∑k=1T(1−p)k−1=1−(1−p)Tp.\displaystyle w_{T}(p)=\sum_{k=1}^{T}(1-p)^{k-1}=\frac{1-(1-p)^{T}}{p}.

Proof. From Equation (7), we have:

∇θJMaxRL(T)​(x)=∑k=1T1k​∇θpass​@​k​(x).\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J^{(T)}_{\textsc{MaxRL}}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{T}\frac{1}{k}\nabla_{\theta}\mathrm{pass@}k(x).

Using pass​@​k​(x)=1−(1−p)k\mathrm{pass@}k(x)=1-(1-p)^{k} where p=pθpass​(x)p=p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x):

∇θpass​@​k​(x)=k​(1−p)k−1​∇θp.\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathrm{pass@}k(x)=k(1-p)^{k-1}\nabla_{\theta}p.

Substituting:

∇θJMaxRL(T)​(x)=∑k=1T1k⋅k​(1−p)k−1​∇θp=(∑k=1T(1−p)k−1)​∇θp=wT​(p)​∇θpθpass​(x).\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J^{(T)}_{\textsc{MaxRL}}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{T}\frac{1}{k}\cdot k(1-p)^{k-1}\nabla_{\theta}p=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{T}(1-p)^{k-1}\right)\nabla_{\theta}p=w_{T}(p)\nabla_{\theta}p^{\mathrm{pass}}_{\theta}(x).

Taking the expectation over x∼ρx\sim\rho completes the proof. ∎

Appendix F RL Implementation Details for LLM Experiments

Our discussion here follows that of Shafayat et al. (2025). For continuity with existing literature, we use slightly different notations from the rest of the paper for this section. Let xx represent a prompt, and let y∼π(⋅|x)y\sim\pi(\cdot|x) represent sequence of tokens autoregressively sampled from the language model π\pi conditioned on the prompt xx. Let πθ\pi_{\theta} be the current policy, and πθold\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} be an older policy (from earlier iterations in training) used for data generation. In our implementation (based on verl (Zhang et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2024)), we use the following general RL objective:

𝒥(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟,{yi}i=1G∼πθold(⋅|x)[1T∑i=1G∑t=1|yi|min(\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ \{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot|x)}\Bigg[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}\min\Big( wi,t(θ)A^i,t,clip(wi,t(θ), 1−ε, 1+ε)A^i,t)]\displaystyle w_{i,t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{i,t},\text{clip}(w_{i,t}(\theta),\ 1-\varepsilon,\ 1+\varepsilon)\hat{A}_{i,t}\Big)\Bigg]

where TT is the total number of tokens in the mini-batch (excluding tokens in the prompt etc., since we only compute loss on the model generated tokens), πθ\pi_{\theta} represents the current LLM’s autoregressive probability distribution, πθold\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} denotes the behavior policy/data generation policy’s probability distribution, wi,t​(θ)w_{i,t}(\theta) is the importance ratio, defined as:

wi,t​(θ)=πθ​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t)πθold​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t)w_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,\ y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,\ y_{i,<t})}

Since we operate fully on-policy, i.e., one RL step per one batch of generated rollouts, this is always one in our experiments, and the clipping parameter ϵ\epsilon has no effect on our training. A^i,t\hat{A}_{i,t} represents the advantage for the tt-th token in the sequence yiy_{i}. The same advantage defined at a sequence level is applied to each token in the sequence, so henceforth we will drop the tt from the notation as well.

The main difference between GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), RLOO (Ahmadian et al., 2024) and MaxRL comes from their use of different advantage functions. RLOO objective uses the following advantage function:

A^iRLOO​R​(y(i),x)−1G−1​∑j≠iR⁡(y(j),x)\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{RLOO}}R(y_{(i)},x)-\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\neq i}R(y_{(j)},x)

whereas GRPO uses the following advantage function:

A^iGRPO=r⁡(x,yi)−mean​({r⁡(x,yi)}i=1G)std​({r⁡(x,yi)}i=1G)+ϵ\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\frac{r(x,y_{i})-\text{mean}\left(\{r(x,y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{G}\right)}{\text{std}\left(\{r(x,y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{G}\right)+\epsilon}

where ϵ\epsilon is a small number (1×10−61\times 10^{-6}) added to avoid division by zero. Finally, the advantage for MaxRL is as follows:

A^iMaxRL=r⁡(x,yi)−mean​({r⁡(x,yi)}i=1G)mean​({r⁡(x,yi)}i=1G)+ϵ\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{\textsc{MaxRL}}}=\frac{r(x,y_{i})-\text{mean}\left(\{r(x,y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{G}\right)}{\text{mean}\left(\{r(x,y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{G}\right)+\epsilon}

Here GG is the number of online samples generated. RLOO, GRPO and MaxRL create a dynamic baseline for each sample without needing a separate value function (unlike PPO (Schulman et al., 2017)), effectively estimating the expected return on-the-fly during training. Not having a value network makes the training much simpler for all three algorithms.

Appendix G Pass@k Calculation

G.1 Closed-form Calculation for Differentiable Settings

To calculate pass@k from a generative model, one usually samples T≥kT\geq k rollouts from the model, calculate success or failure from each of them, and then uses an appropriate statistical estimator for pass@k (Chen et al., 2021; Yue et al., 2025). However, since there is no latent reasoning process involved in our didactic ImageNet experiments and since we can directly calculate the model likelihood of label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} for an input image x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, namely πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x), we can also analytically compute pass@k without sampling as well. Formally, in all ImageNet experiments, we calculate pass@k for an example (image, label) pair (x,y∗​(x))(x,y^{\ast}(x)) as follows:

Pass​@​k​(x,y∗​(x),πθ)=1−(1−πθ​(y∗​(x)|x))k\text{Pass}@k(x,y^{\ast}(x);\pi_{\theta})=1-(1-\pi_{\theta}(y^{\ast}(x)|x))^{k}

The average pass@k is then obtained by averaging the above quantity over all example pairs in the validation dataset.

G.2 Sampling-based Estimator

Unlike the ImageNet setting, we can’t usually directly calculate pass@k via accessing the true probability of the correct action. Therefore, we use the default pass@k calculation mechanism in verl (Sheng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), using the bootstrapping low variance unbiased estimator introduced by Chen et al. (2021). This employs generating n≥kn\geq k samples per task, counting the number of correct samples c⁡(x)c(x) among the nn samples, and estimate pass@k as:

Pass​@​k=𝔼x∼ρ​[1−(n−c⁡(x)k)(nk)]\text{Pass}@k=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c(x)}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right]

Appendix H ImageNet Experiments

H.1 Training Procedure

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the input space and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be the label space. Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote our model: given an input image x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, πθ​(y|x)\pi_{\theta}(y|x) is the model’s predicted probability of image xx belonging to class y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. For an input image and label pair (x,y∗​(x))(x,y^{\ast}(x)), the cross-entropy loss is:

ℒCE​(x,y∗​(x),πθ)=−log⁡πθ​(y∗​(x)|x)\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(x,y^{\ast}(x);\pi_{\theta})=-\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{\ast}(x)|x)

On the other hand, the corresponding RL objective for the same pair is:

ℒRL(x,y∗;πθ)=−𝔼y∼πθ(⋅|x)[logπθ(y|x)⋅A^(y|x)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{RL}}(x,y^{\ast};\pi_{\theta})=-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot\hat{A}(y|x)]

where the expectation is computed using Monte-Carlo sampling with KK rollouts of yy from πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x). GRPO, REINFORCE and MaxRL vary only in the calculation of the advantage A⁡(y|x)A(y|x). Concretely, let y(1),…,y(K)y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(K)} be our KK rollouts, sampled from the conditional probability distribution πθ(⋅|x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x). We operate under a binary reward setting, meaning the reward function r⁡(x,y)r(x,y) is:

r(x,y)=𝕀[y=y∗(x)]={1,if ​y=y∗​(x)0,otherwiser(x,y)=\mathbb{I}[y=y^{\ast}(x)]=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }y=y^{\ast}(x)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

Given this reward, we calculate advantage under GRPO, REINFORCE and MaxRL as follows:

A^GRPO​(x,y)=r⁡(x,y)−μ^σ^\hat{A}_{\text{GRPO}}(x,y)=\frac{r(x,y)-\hat{\mu}}{\hat{\sigma}}
A^REINFORCE​(x,y)=r⁡(x,y)−μ^\hat{A}_{\text{REINFORCE}}(x,y)=r(x,y)-\hat{\mu}
A^MaxRL​(x,y)=r⁡(x,y)−μ^μ^\hat{A}_{\textsc{MaxRL}}(x,y)=\frac{r(x,y)-\hat{\mu}}{\hat{\mu}}

where μ^=∑i=1Kr⁡(x,y(i))K\hat{\mu}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}r(x,y^{(i)})}{K}, σ^=∑i=1K(r⁡(x,y(i))−μ^)2K\hat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}(r(x,y^{(i)})-\hat{\mu})^{2}}{K}} are the mean and standard deviation of rewards of the sampled rollouts.

Finally, at each training step, a batch of (input image, label) pairs is collected from the training dataset. The above computation gives us per (input image, label) loss, we average them over all the pairs in a given batch to calculate the final loss which is then used to update the model via gradient descent.

H.2 Training Hyperparameters

We train ResNet-50 (He et al., 2016) models on ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) with a batch size of 256256 for 2020 epochs using SGD with momentum 0.90.9 (no Nesterov momentum) and an initial learning rate of 0.10.1. We swept the learning rate over {0.001,0.003,0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,0.7,1.0}\{0.001,0.003,0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,0.7,1.0\} and found that the standard value of 0.10.1 generally works well for all objectives, so we report results at this setting. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) with linear warmup for the first epoch. For evaluation, no augmentation is applied: each image is resized to 224×224224\times 224 and normalized by the channel-wise mean and standard deviation of pixel values. During training, in addition to the same resizing and normalization, we apply a random horizontal flip (with probability 0.50.5) and a random resized crop to 224×224224\times 224 (with scale (0.08,1.0)(0.08,1.0)). The number of rollouts KK is varied across experiments. All training runs are conducted on a single L40S GPU for 15 hours.

H.3 Equivalence of Validation Top-1 Accuracy and Majority Voting Accuracy

In this section, we discuss the validation top-1 accuracy metric, which is the traditional metric used in image classification. Formally, validation accuracy for a single image and label pair (x,y∗​(x))(x,y^{\ast}(x)) is defined as:

Accuracy(x,y∗(x);πθ)=𝕀[argmaxy∈𝒴πθ(y|x)=y∗(x)]={1,if ​arg⁡maxy∈𝒴​πθ​(y|x)=y∗​(x)0,otherwise\text{Accuracy}(x,y^{\ast}(x);\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{I}\left[\arg\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)=y^{\ast}(x)\right]=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\arg\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)=y^{\ast}(x)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

which is then averaged over all validation examples for the final metric. In other words, validation accuracy is the same as majority voting accuracy (Wang et al., 2023a) in traditional LLM chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.

H.4 Gradient Norm Analysis

Fig. 9 shows the correlation between gradient norm and pass rate (model’s predicted probability of the correct class) for a particular image on different objectives. We see that cross-entropy and MaxRL have a similar scatter plot: with high gradient norm for hard inputs (pass rate close to 0) and lower gradient norm for the easier ones (pass rate close to 1). In contrast, the highest gradient norm for GRPO is on medium-difficulty (pass rate close to 0.5) inputs, with hard inputs having very low gradient norm.

Finally, REINFORCE fails to produce any significant gradient norm compared to the other objectives and its pass rate is confined below 0.003 after 1500 steps, demonstrating its difficulty to learn in this setting. This is also reflected in our other results, where REINFORCE does not show any signs of learning. We attribute this to the very low gradient norm: since the randomly initialized model has pass rate 0.0010.001 in expectation over all inputs, REINFORCE fails to produce sufficiently large gradients during training and therefore stalls in model improvement. One caveat: REINFORCE’s failure may be due to us training the model from scratch — on a pretrained model, it indeed produces gradients but still shows poor gradient norm on hard inputs (see Fig. 7).

H.5 Comparison with GRPO and Additional Metrics

Here we present additional experimental results. In particular, (1) we compare against GRPO with varying number of rollouts, (2) record additional metrics such as majority voting accuracy (i.e., validation top-1 accuracy), and (3) show the resulting coverage (pass@k vs k) from different objectives. Fig. 10 records our findings: MaxRL outperforms and scales better than GRPO with additional compute. While GRPO improves performance if given more compute unlike REINFORCE, it remains suboptimal compared to MaxRL and supervised cross-entropy training. Moreover, both GRPO and REINFORCE exhibit worse coverage as their pass@k values are significantly lower compared to MaxRL, corroborating our experiments from other sections.

Appendix I Maze Experiments

I.1 Model Architecture

We adopt a lightweight decoder-only Transformer model following the Qwen2 architecture (Yang et al., 2024a), with a total of approximately 3​M3M parameters. The model consists of 4 Transformer layers, each using full self-attention. The hidden size is set to 256, with an intermediate (feed-forward) dimension of 1024, and 4 attention heads per layer. We use grouped query attention with 2 key-value heads. The model employs RMSNorm with σ=1×10−6\sigma=1\times 10^{-6} and uses the SiLU activation function in the feed-forward networks. Rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024) are applied with θ=1,000,000\theta=1,000,000, and the maximum sequence length is 512 tokens. The vocabulary size is 32 tokens, and input and output embeddings are tied. The model is trained and evaluated using bfloat16 precision, with attention dropout set to 0. The architecture follows a standard causal language modeling setup with autoregressive decoding.

I.2 Task Description

Mazes are procedurally generated using Prim’s algorithm (Prim, 1957), and task difficulty is controlled by the grid size. We use a symbolic tokenization to represent both the maze layout and the navigation policy, with tokens drawn from a small, discrete vocabulary.

The input sequence describes a two-dimensional grid in row-major order. Each cell is represented by a single token indicating its type (e.g., WALL, PATH, START, or GOAL). Rows are separated by a dedicated NEWLINE token, and the entire grid is delimited by special boundary tokens marking the beginning (GRID_START) and end (GRID_END) of the grid description. Following the maze specification, the model autoregressively generates a sequence of navigation actions drawn from a fixed action vocabulary (e.g., directional moves) and terminates by a DONE token.

Below, we provide an example data instance following this format.

For reference, we also visualize one typical successful trajectory and one representative failed prediction in Figure 11.

I.3 Training Setups

To ensure sufficient task complexity and rigorous evaluation, we construct a training set of 1 million distinct 17×1717\times 17 mazes and a test set of 256 non-overlapping samples. We first pretrain the model from scratch, where it is trained to follow a provided ground-truth trajectory for each maze. During SFT, we use a learning rate of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} with the AdamW optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) and train for 1,500 steps with a batch size of 32. This pretraining stage44 4 Our pretrained Maze transformer checkpoint, which is used as the starting model for RL fine-tuning, can be found here: https://github.com/tajwarfahim/maxrl/tree/main/maze/ckpt-1500. initializes the model with the basic output format required for representing maze-solving trajectories.

Subsequently, we perform reinforcement learning (RL) training, where we use a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} in all our experiments. We update the model parameters only once per RL step (i.e., the fully on-policy setting from  Tajwar et al. (2024)). We have two different training settings:

  1. 1.

    256 Batch size, 9000 RL steps, varying number of training rollouts. This is used for Figs. 4 and 12. Fig. 4 compares performance across different number of training rollouts (from 4 to 128). We observed that when number of training rollouts is sufficiently small (e.g., 4), lower batch size training runs can collapse, possibly due to noise/gradient variance. Hence these runs use a larger batch size of 256. Since this setting is very expensive, we only train our models for 9000 RL steps, and only train with MaxRL and our principal baselines, namely GRPO and RLOO. Fig. 12 shows the evolution of various Pass@k metrics under these 3 objectives during training, and reports experiments resulting from our highest compute setting, namely that with 128 training rollouts per prompt.

  2. 2.

    32 Batch size, 20000 RL steps, 128 training rollouts per task. This setting is used for Fig. 13, where we show the training curves for different baselines on the maze setting, and Table 2, where we present summary Pass@k performance of different baselines at the end of 20000 training steps. Our first setting of 256 batch size was beyond our compute budget for being too expensive to train all the different baselines with, so we adopted this cheaper setting for baseline comparison.

Each training run uses 4 RTX 4090 GPUs. Given the small number of model parameters, the model is no longer memory-bound, so we modified the rollout engine (instead of using the default vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) engine) in the verl (Zhang et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2024) codebase to increase sampling parallelism and speed up training.

I.4 Training Dynamics in Our Highest Compute Budget Setting

Here we provide additional results pertaining to the training dynamics of MaxRL in the infinite data maze setting. Figure 12 shows pass@1 through pass@256 over training steps for MaxRL, GRPO, and RLOO, trained for 9000 RL steps using 256 batch size and 128 training rollouts per task. MaxRL outperforms both GRPO and RLOO at all metrics.

I.5 Comparison Table with Additional Baselines

Table 2 compares MaxRL against a broader set of baselines in the Maze setting, where all models are trained for 20,000 steps with a batch size of 32 and 128 rollouts per prompt. MaxRL reaches 84.484.4 pass@1 and 94.394.3 pass@256, improving over standard GRPO by more than 4444 points on pass@1. PKPO attains a strong pass@1 of 74.574.5 but its pass@k curve is nearly flat, indicating that it has largely collapsed onto a single mode and gains little from additional samples. SELF reaches a high pass@256 of 87.587.5 yet a weak pass@1 of 46.146.1, trading away average accuracy for coverage. GRPO, with or without an entropy bonus, and Differential Smoothing all remain well below 6060 across the board; among these, Differential Smoothing performs slightly better than GRPO with an entropy bonus, which in turn improves over vanilla GRPO. Fig. 13 shows the evolution of the Pass@k metrics for these baselines throughout during. Overall, MaxRL shows superior performance on both average accuracy (pass@1) and coverage (pass@k).

Appendix J GSM8K Experiments

J.1 Prompt template

The goal of this experiment setting is to study how RL algorithms perform in data-scarce but compute rich settings. This is similar in spirit to Kim et al. (2026), except that we study RL and not pre-training. Due to our compute limitations, we choose a relatively small model (360M parameters) for our experiments. Specifically, we conduct reinforcement finetuning on the SmolLM2-360M-Instruct model (Allal et al., 2025) using the GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) training set for 1500 steps. We use GSM8K-Platinum (Vendrow et al., 2025), a revised version of the original GSM8K test that is non-overlapping with the GSM8K train dataset, for evaluation. An example prompt and the model’s response are shown below. In particular, we take each individual problem, append it with “ Let’s think step by step and output the final answer within \\boxed{}." and process the string through the SmolLM2-360M-Instruct model’s tokenizer chat-template to obtain the final prompt for the model.

J.2 Hyperparameters

Detailed hyperparameter setup is provided in Table 3. For other baselines, we use T=16T=16 for PKPO, which means we optimize pass@16 as the objective, and γ=0.05\gamma=0.05 for differential smoothing.

J.3 Effect of Additional Compute

In Fig. 3, we demonstrated how MaxRL’s performance scales as additional compute is available in terms of rollout budget, but in our supervised ImageNet classification setting. Here, we further experiment with the effect of additional compute on the finite data GSM8K training setting, which is a more realistic RL training since it involves autoregressive generations from a 360M LLM on a real mathematical reasoning task.

Fig. 14 shows our findings: as the number of training rollouts increases, it results in performance improvement in the final checkpoint. Moreover, as expected, the biggest gains come at higher values of pass@k, with T=128T=128 outperforming T=1T=1 (REINFORCE) by almost 30%30\% at pass@2048.

J.4 Comparison with Additional Baselines

Table 4 compares MaxRL against the same set of baselines in the data-scarce GSM8K training setting (Table 3). MaxRL again achieves the best performance on every metric, reaching 33.233.2 pass@1 and 83.483.4 pass@1024. While all methods are clustered within a few points at pass@1 (between 27.527.5 and 33.233.2), the differences widen dramatically as kk grows: MaxRL attains 83.483.4 pass@1024, 7.57.5 points above the strongest baseline (PKPO at 75.975.9) and more than 3030 points above GRPO, RLOO, GRPO with an entropy bonus, and Differential Smoothing, all of which saturate around 4949–5252. These results suggest MaxRL extracts more learning signal from a fixed training dataset.

J.5 Per-Prompt Pass-Rate Distribution During Training

To visualize the sharpening dynamics of the three methods, Fig. 15 tracks the empirical distribution of per-prompt pass rates over the GSM8K training set throughout the SmolLM2-360M-Instruct run from Table 3. Each row corresponds to a training epoch (0,10,20,30,40,500,10,20,30,40,50), each column to a method, and each bar to the fraction of training prompts whose pass-rate estimate falls into the corresponding log2\log_{2}-spaced bin (with the leftmost bin reserved for prompts with 00 correct rollouts and the rightmost for prompts solved on every rollout). Validation pass@1 values of the corresponding checkpoints over the entire evaluation dataset are reported on top of each panel.

Fig. 15 suggests that GRPO and RLOO push the per-prompt pass-rate distribution towards either 0 or 1, supporting the distribution sharpening narrative, whereas MaxRL retains a broad distribution of pass rates throughout training. This contrast shows that MaxRL is more robust to the distribution sharpening commonly observed in LLM reinforcement learning (Yue et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), allowing it to extract more learning signal from a fixed training dataset.

Appendix K Qwen3 Experiments

K.1 Prompt template

We use the Qwen-math template (Yang et al., 2024a; Qwen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024b) for formatting our prompts. We show an example prompt (Yu et al., 2025) after formatting through our template below. In particular, we take each individual problem, append it with “\nPlease reason step by step, and put your final answer within \\boxed{{}}." and process the string through the Qwen3 model’s tokenizer chat-template to obtain the final prompt for the model.

K.2 Hyperparameters

Next, we describe the default hyperparameters for our training setup. Since there are many possible alternatives to handle off-policy updates and corresponding importance ratio (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; MiniMax et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), to keep things simple, we choose to train in the fully on-policy setup, meaning we have no importance ratio or associated clipping. Similarly, to avoid tuning additional hyperparameters for each algorithm, following Olmo et al. (2025), we remove KL penalty and also entropy bonus in our default training comparison. Note: we train with GRPO and entropy bonus as a baseline in our SmolLM2-360M-Instruct training on GSM8K, results are recorded in Table 4: MaxRL outperforms this variant, showing that entropy bonus does not fully mitigate issues resulting from GRPO though it can slightly mitigate it, as also observed by Yue et al. (2025).

We generate all training rollouts using temperature 1.0, and do not use special sampling techniques. Similarly, we also do not use any adaptive sampling (Yu et al., 2025) or fixes for inference-training logit mismatch (He, 2025; Khatri et al., 2026). Finally, for evaluation, we follow the same protocol as Yue et al. (2025), and we run inference with temperature 0.6, top-p sampling parameter 0.95, no top-k or min-p sampling (Nguyen et al., 2025a).

Table 5 shows our default hyperparameter setting.

K.3 Additional Results

We report additional empirical results from our Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base training runs that complement the main-paper evaluation. We expand the benchmark coverage with four further reasoning datasets, compare MaxRL against the base model and GRPO under verifier-free majority voting, and report training-dynamics traces (response length, actor entropy, gradient norm) as well as validation pass@1 curves throughout training.

Extended Benchmarks

Beyond the four primary benchmarks reported in the main paper, we further evaluate the Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base trained models on four additional reasoning benchmarks: AIME 2024, HMMT Feb 2025 (MathArena, 2025a), HMMT Nov 2025 (MathArena, 2025b), and JEEBENCH (Arora et al., 2023). Fig. 16 reports coverage on these benchmarks; MaxRL matches or outperforms both the base model and GRPO, achieving up to 20.5×20.5\times speedup over GRPO when generating multiple samples under a perfect verifier while maintaining similar or better pass@1 performance.

Majority voting

We compare MaxRL against the base model and GRPO under majority voting (Wang et al., 2023a), a widely used verifier-free method for scaling test-time compute: we draw NN i.i.d. rollouts for each prompt, group the responses by their final answer, and take the most frequent answer as our prediction. Table 6 reports majority-voting accuracy on five benchmarks; MaxRL outperforms both the pretrained base model and the GRPO-trained model on every benchmark.

Training dynamics

We record mean generated response length, actor entropy, and gradient norm throughout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base (Fig. 17) and Qwen3-1.7B-Base (Fig. 18). The trends are consistent across model sizes: MaxRL produces longer chains-of-thought, retains higher actor entropy, and exhibits larger gradient norms during training compared with GRPO.

Validation accuracy during training

In addition, we examine pass@1 (estimated using 32 samples) over the course of training on intermediate evaluation datasets. For Qwen3-4B-Base, MaxRL consistently outperforms GRPO across the three evaluation datasets (Fig. 19). For the smaller Qwen3-1.7B-Base model (Fig. 20), MaxRL initially trails GRPO at pass@1, similar to the SmolLM curve in Fig. 5, but catches up with extended training and ultimately converges to a higher value.

Appendix L Comparison with Additional Baselines

L.1 PKPO

Realizing the shortcomings of the expected reward (pass@1) optimization paradigm in reinforcement learning, recent work (Walder and Karkhanis, 2025; Tang et al., 2025; Bagirov et al., 2025) has also proposed directly optimizing for pass@k during RL training. The connection between maximum likelihood and harmonic mixture of pass@k optimization necessitates a direct comparison between our work and these pass@k optimization procedures. Here we present comparisons with a representative baseline, PKPO (Walder and Karkhanis, 2025). PKPO has a tunable hyperparameter TT, which dictates the order of optimization objective, namely PKPO with parameter TT optimizes pass@TT directly.

Tables 7 and 8 show comparison between PKPO and MaxRL on the maze and GSM8K settings, respectively. PKPO experiments are run with T=16T=16, with all other hyperparameters kept the same as their default values for the respective settings. We observe that MaxRL outperforms PKPO at all values of pass@k. More importantly, MaxRL outperforms PKPO at pass@16, despite the latter explicitly optimizing for this metric. A similar phenomenon is observed with REINFORCE, which directly optimizes pass@1 yet consistently underperforms MaxRL at pass@1. This suggests that directly optimizing a specific pass@k objective does not necessarily yield the best performance at that pass@k. We hypothesize that MaxRL’s aggregation of signals across pass@k events enables more effective use of the learning signal, and leave a detailed investigation to future work.

Fig. 21 shows further comparisons against PKPO on the large scale LLM training setting. Specifically, we train a Qwen3-4B-Base model on the POLARIS-53K dataset, using the default hyperparameters for this setting. For PKPO, we train with 3 different values of TT, namely 4, 8, and 16. MaxRL retains similar performance or outperforms PKPO on all 4 evaluation datasets. On harder evaluation datasets like BeyondAIME and AIME 2025, the gap is more pronounced, and MaxRL outperforms PKPO at pass@k for all values of k that we evaluated on. These large-scale training experiments validate our results from the smaller maze and GSM8K settings.

L.2 ZPD

One way of thinking about MaxRL is to focus on its upweighting of high-difficulty prompts. This raises the question: how does MaxRL compare to methods that perform difficulty-aware sampling strategies? RLOO with a “not too easy, not too hard" curriculum (ZPD (Bae et al., 2026)) can be interpreted as reweighting prompts with weight w⁡(p)=p⁡(1−p)w(p)=p(1-p), where p=pθ​(x)p=p_{\theta}(x) is the pass rate for prompt xx, in Fig. 1. Since we do not use any additional curriculum learning or involved sampling strategies in our setting for the sake of simplicity, we choose to compare against this variant of ZPD by employing the advantage function A^​(x,y)=r^​(1−r^)​(r⁡(x,y)−r^)\hat{A}(x,y)=\hat{r}(1-\hat{r})(r(x,y)-\hat{r}), where r^\hat{r} is the Monte-Carlo estimate of the pass rate for prompt xx.

First, we compare against ZPD on the ImageNet classification setting in Fig. 22. ZPD performs similarly to REINFORCE here, and fails to improve the model significantly beyond its random initialization at the beginning of training.

Next, we evaluate ZPD on the maze and GSM8K training settings. Fig. 23 shows our main results: under identical training settings and compute budget, MaxRL outperforms ZPD on both settings, achieving significantly higher pass@k for all values of k that we evaluated on. On GSM8K, MaxRL achieves ∼30%\sim 30\% improvement in pass@2048 over ZPD.

Finally, we also compared MaxRL with ZPD on our largest training setting: Qwen3-4B-Base trained on POLARIS-53K. Fig. 24 shows our main findings: under identical training setup and compute budget (1000 steps of RL training), MaxRL outperforms ZPD on all evaluation datasets, achieving gains of 12.6×\times to 29.0×\times in test-time scaling efficiency under a perfect verifier.

L.3 Power Function

Finally, MaxRL can be seen as optimizing a particular non-linear function of the pass rate (log⁡pθ​(x)\log p_{\theta}(x)). This begs the question of how other non-linear functions of the pass rate may perform. Here we compare with an example function from Xiong et al. (2025b), namely, the Power Function weighting. The Power Function with parameter α>0\alpha>0 is defined as f⁡(t)=tαf(t)=t^{\alpha}, and correspondingly one can optimize Jpower−functionα=𝔼x∼ρ​[pθ​(x)]αJ_{\mathrm{power-function}}^{\alpha}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}[p_{\theta}(x)]^{\alpha}. The corresponding gradient of this objective is:

∇θJpower−functionα=𝔼x∼ρ​[α​pθ​(x)α−1​∇θpθ​(x)]\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{power-function}}^{\alpha}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[\alpha p_{\theta}(x)^{\alpha-1}\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(x)\right]

where ∇θpθ​(x)\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(x) is the standard REINFORCE gradient. Xiong et al. (2025b) particularly considers power functions with α=12\alpha=\frac{1}{2}, giving the following gradient:

∇θJpower−function=𝔼x∼ρ​[12​pθ​(x)​∇θpθ​(x)]\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{power-function}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p_{\theta}(x)}}\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(x)\right]

In practice, this objective can be optimized by setting the advantage to be A^​(x,y)=r⁡(x,y)−r^2​r^\hat{A}(x,y)=\frac{r(x,y)-\hat{r}}{2\sqrt{\hat{r}}} when r^>0\hat{r}>0 and 0 otherwise, with r^\hat{r} being the Monte-Carlo estimate of the pass rate for prompt xx. This is the variant of the Power Function objective that we will compare MaxRL against in this work.

First, we compare against this version of the Power Function on our supervised ImageNet classification setting under an identical training recipe. Fig. 25 shows our empirical findings: MaxRL outperforms Power Function at both pass@1 and pass@128 despite using 128x less rollout compute budget. Moreover, the gap is higher for pass@128, showing that despite performing better than REINFORCE and GRPO in this setting, ultimately the Power Function is a suboptimal choice compared to MaxRL here.

Next, we scale up our comparisons to the infinite training data maze and finite training data GSM8K settings using identical training hyperparameters and compute budget. Fig. 26 summarizes our main findings: MaxRL outperforms this variant of the Power Function objective on both settings. MaxRL achieves significantly higher pass@k on both settings, and outperforms Power Function by ∼20%\sim 20\% at pass@2048 on GSM8K.

Finally, we also compared MaxRL against the Power Function on our largest training setting: Qwen3-4B-Base trained on POLARIS-53K. Fig. 27 shows our main findings: under identical training setup and compute budget (1000 steps of RL training), MaxRL matches or outperforms Power Function on all 4 evaluation datasets, achieving up to 12.4×\times test-time scaling efficiency gains under a perfect verifier.

Appendix M Additional Analyses

M.1 Non-Zero Gradient Signal Analysis

A prompt for which the model fails to generate any correct rollout contributes no gradient under REINFORCE, GRPO, RLOO, or MaxRL, since the advantage vanishes when every sampled return equals the empirical baseline. We extend the analysis in Fig. 8 from the large-scale LLM settings to the maze and SmolLM2-360M-Instruct on GSM8K training settings, and record this fraction throughout training in Fig. 28. MaxRL consistently produces at least one correct rollout for a larger fraction of prompts than GRPO and RLOO across both settings, and the gap persists as training progresses. This matches the trends observed in the large-scale experiments and offers a complementary view on why MaxRL continues to improve when REINFORCE-style baselines stall: by upweighting harder prompts and producing larger gradient norms on them (Fig. 7), MaxRL keeps a larger fraction of the dataset contributing useful gradient signal even after the easier prompts have saturated.

M.2 Policy Gradient Variance Analysis

In this section, we analyze the variance of policy-gradient estimates for MaxRL and other methods, focusing on two questions: (1) does the baseline in our estimator (Equation 10) actually reduce variance, and (2) how does estimator noise scale with the number of rollouts for MaxRL?

We first study the effect of the control variate in MaxRL. Note that using the unconditional average score function as the baseline is not guaranteed to reduce variance. Previous work such as Greensmith et al. (2004) has noted that this can indeed be suboptimal even for the canonical REINFORCE objective, and provides the derivation of an optimal baseline. However, computing the optimal baseline is complicated in practice, and the average score function as the standard choice of baseline is empirically justified and widely used (Ahmadian et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025a). In this section, we follow the same direction and provide empirical proof that the variance reduction technique used by us indeed reduces variance in practical scenarios. Using the rollout pools from the previous experiments, we estimate the trace of the sample covariance matrix across policy-gradient minibatches, following prior work (McCandlish et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2025a). Given BB independently sampled minibatch gradient estimates {gb}b=1B\{g_{b}\}_{b=1}^{B}, we compute

𝒱^​(g)=tr⁡(Cov^​(g))=1B−1​∑b=1B‖gb−g¯‖22,g¯=1B​∑b=1Bgb,\widehat{\mathcal{V}}(g)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(g)\right)=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\|g_{b}-\bar{g}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\bar{g}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}g_{b},

where each gbg_{b} is the flattened policy-gradient vector for one sampled minibatch. Specifically, for GSM8K and Polaris-53K, we use 16 prompts with 512 pre-generated rollouts per prompt; for Maze, we use 256 prompts with 1024 rollouts per prompt. For each N∈{4,8,16,32,64,128}N\in\{4,8,16,32,64,128\}, we randomly subsample B=4B=4 minibatches with NN rollouts per prompt and report 𝒱^​(g)\widehat{\mathcal{V}}(g). Figure 29 shows that the baseline consistently lowers the variance of the MaxRL gradient estimator across rollout counts and tasks. The baseline is most important when number of rollouts is low, and eventually for high enough rollout count the gradient variance with and without baseline seems to converge, as expected.

We next study how the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of policy gradients scales with the number of rollouts for MaxRL, GRPO, and RLOO. Since these methods optimize different objectives, raw variance is not directly comparable across methods. We therefore normalize by the squared norm of the expected gradient and report inverse signal-to-noise ratio, tr⁡(Cov⁡(g))‖𝔼⁡[g]‖22\textstyle\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Cov}(g))}{\|\mathbb{E}[g]\|_{2}^{2}}, where lower values indicate a more accurate gradient estimate relative to its signal. On ImageNet, we estimate this quantity using ResNet-50 gradients over a fixed batch of 1024 images and 64 gradient samples per rollout count. For Maze, we sample 8 prompt batches of 256 prompts from the pre-generated rollout table and estimate inverse SNR from 64 randomized rollout minibatches. For SmolLM on GSM8K, we fix one batch of 64 prompts and form 64 gradient samples through repeated rollout subsampling. Figure 30 shows that the normalized variance of MaxRL decreases as NN increases, following the same qualitative trend as GRPO and RLOO.

Together, these results suggest that the proposed baseline reduces the raw variance of the MaxRL estimator. They also show that the stability of MaxRL improves as the rollout budget increases, despite its stronger amplification of very-low-success-rate problems.

M.3 On the Distribution Sharpening Narrative

Recent work (Yue et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026) has shown that RL trained models can underperform base models at pass@k, and thereby under a high sampling budget coupled with a perfect verifier, base models can solve a larger number of problems than their RL-trained counterpart. We saw in our experiments that contrary to the standard REINFORCE and GRPO objectives, MaxRL increases pass@k even for very large values of k beyond that of the base model in a majority of scenarios and especially if we do not overtrain. The natural next question to ask is whether MaxRL can lead to expansion of capability beyond the base model. Since any sequence of tokens that lead to the correct answer has a non-zero probability under any language model, we instead ask this question from a finite compute perspective: if one has a large but finite compute, what fraction of the problems can one solve with the base model, and its GRPO- and MaxRL-trained counterparts?

Table 9 shows the results of empirical study. Specifically, we take the Qwen3-4B-Base model, and its final GRPO and MaxRL trained checkpoints after 1000 steps of RL training. Next, we generate 4096 rollouts for each of the 30 questions in the AIME 2025 dataset, from each of these 3 models. We list the indices of the problems where each model generates at least 1 correct solution from its 4096 rollouts. We see that the problems solved by the base model and GRPO-trained model are strict subsets of the problem set solved by MaxRL. Moreover, MaxRL solves 3 additional problems exclusively that are not solved by either the base model or the GRPO-trained model.

Beyond Table 9, we also provide additional evidence in the form of perplexity analysis. Specifically, Fig. 31 shows that on the 3 problems from AIME 2025 that only our MaxRL-trained checkpoint could solve, the 15 correct rollouts have very high perplexity under the base and GRPO trained checkpoint. As a control set, we also record perplexity of an equal number of incorrect rollouts generated from the base model, and show that they have much lower perplexity than the MaxRL-generated correct trajectories. Overall, we believe that MaxRL can induce capabilities beyond what is present in the base model, and leave further studying this for future work.

M.4 Non-Binary Reward Settings

Our work focuses on binary correctness-based rewards, where the connection to maximum likelihood is most direct. While the binary reward setting already captures a broad and practically important class of RL problems, including applications such as improving complex reasoning in LLMs (e.g., math and code generation) (Zeng et al., 2025b; Mroueh, 2026; Luo et al., 2025) and robotics (Liu et al., 2023; Herzog et al., 2023; Kalashnikov et al., 2018), here we study non-binary reward settings for the sake of completeness.

Interestingly, MaxRL admits a natural extension to non-binary reward settings under mild assumptions. In particular, for non-negative rewards with non-zero expectation under the policy (i.e., 𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)]>0\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)]>0), we can generalize the MaxRL objective from

log𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[𝕀[y=y∗]]\log\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[\mathbb{I}[y=y^{\ast}]]

to

log𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)]\log\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)]

This yields a gradient estimator analogous to MaxRL, with advantage:

A⁡(x,yi)=r⁡(x,yi)−μ^μ^A(x,y_{i})=\frac{r(x,y_{i})-\hat{\mu}}{\hat{\mu}}

where μ^\hat{\mu} is the Monte-Carlo estimate of 𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)]\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)].

We have evaluated this extension on a modified version of the Maze task with continuous rewards r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1], where shorter trajectories receive higher rewards. Specifically, for maze xx, let Li​(x)L_{i}(x) denote the length of the ii-th rollout, Lmin​(x)L_{\mathrm{min}}(x) denote the shortest possible path length, and TT denote the maximum trajectory length possible (usually equal to the token limit for each generation). We define

ri=T−Li​(x)T−Lmin​(x)r_{i}=\frac{T-L_{i}(x)}{T-L_{\mathrm{min}}(x)}

In this setting, we train a 16M transformer with batch size 256 and 16 rollouts per task, with all other hyperparameters kept the same as the default values for the maze setting. This extension of MaxRL outperforms GRPO by a large margin on both Mean@32 and Best@32 validation reward. Moreover, in this setting, the Best@32 reward for GRPO has collapsed, showing that training for longer is unlikely to improve for GRPO, whereas both Mean and Best reward are still increasing at the end of training for MaxRL.

While the initial results are encouraging, we leave the full theoretical treatment and broader empirical evaluation of non-binary rewards to future work.
